                    "qid": "question-1kssobnpu",
                    "title": "Are you a data controller or processor processing personal data to which the GDPR applies?",
                    "number": 1,
                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "GDPR applies to you if you are processing personal data in any of the following ways:\n\n(1) Processing personal data of data subjects who are in the EU, where the processing activities are related to the monitoring of the behavior of data subjects as far as their behavior takes place within the EU.\n\n(2) Processing personal data of data subjects who are in the EU, where the processing activities are related to the offering of goods or services, to data subjects in the EU.\n\n(3) Processing personal data in the context of the activities of an establishment in the EU, regardless of whether the processing takes place in the EU or not.\n\n(4) Processing personal data in a place where member state law applies by virtue of public international law when you are not established in the EU.",
                    "mandatory": false,
                    "custom_builder_response": "{\"builder\":[{\"label\":\"Yes/No\",\"hideLabel\":true,\"optionsLabelPosition\":\"right\",\"values\":[{\"label\":\"Yes\",\"value\":\"yes\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"No\",\"value\":\"no\",\"shortcut\":\"\"}],\"customClass\":\"f-boolean-selector\",\"tableView\":true,\"type\":\"radio\",\"key\":\"yesNo\",\"input\":true,\"defaultValue\":\"\",\"multiple\":false,\"refreshOn\":\"\",\"clearOnRefresh\":false,\"placeholder\":\"\"}],\"rules_order\":[],\"responseTypes\":[\"yesNo\"],\"rating_mapping\":null,\"risk_mapping\":null,\"workflow_mapping\":null,\"skip_mapping\":null,\"data_map_metadata\":null}",

                    "additional_details": "The EDPB has mandated all data exporters to undertake a mapping exercise of their data flows. You must know exactly to which jurisdictions your data is being transferred. You must take into account all onward transfers (transfers from non-EEA processors to other non-EEA processors - in the same third country or another) as well as access or storage in a cloud outside of EEA. You must document this process for future auditing purposes.",
                    "mandatory": false,
                    "custom_builder_response": "{\"builder\":[{\"label\":\"Yes/No\",\"hideLabel\":true,\"optionsLabelPosition\":\"right\",\"values\":[{\"label\":\"Yes\",\"value\":\"yes\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"No\",\"value\":\"no\",\"shortcut\":\"\"}],\"customClass\":\"f-boolean-selector\",\"tableView\":true,\"type\":\"radio\",\"key\":\"yesNo\",\"input\":true,\"defaultValue\":\"\",\"multiple\":false,\"refreshOn\":\"\",\"clearOnRefresh\":false,\"placeholder\":\"\"}],\"rules_order\":[\"Set Risk\"],\"responseTypes\":[\"yesNo\"],\"rating_mapping\":null,\"risk_mapping\":{\"rules\":[{\"operator\":\"Equals to\",\"value\":[\"no\"],\"risk\":{\"level\":\"Very High\",\"description\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eIf you do not know to which jurisdictions your data is being sent, you are in violation of the EDPB guidelines on international data transfers.                     "title": "Are you transferring data to a recipient jurisdiction outside the EEA which does not have an adequacy decision by the EU Commission?",

                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "EDPB has mandated additional responsibilities for data exporters and importers for transfers of personal data between the EEA to a jurisdiction that does not have an adequacy decision. This is because countries without an adequacy decision could have surveillance laws or practices which allow public authorities of the jurisdiction unnecessary, disproportionate and overbroad access to the transferred personal data, risking the rights and freedoms of EU residents. Thus these transfers might require supplementary measures for the protection of the personal data from the public authorities of the recipient jurisdiction.",
                    "mandatory": false,

                    "title": "If you are transferring personal data outside the EEA, are these cross-border data transfers limited to what are necessary and adequate?",
                    "number": 4,
                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "The EDPB requires that all data transfers should be analyzed and only minimal and necessary personal data should be transferred which is adequate for the purposes of the processing. This analysis also requires that there are no suitable alternatives to the transfer. Document this analysis for future auditing purposes.",
                    "mandatory": false,
                    "custom_builder_response": "{\"builder\":[{\"label\":\"Yes/No\",\"hideLabel\":true,\"optionsLabelPosition\":\"right\",\"values\":[{\"label\":\"Yes\",\"value\":\"yes\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"No\",\"value\":\"no\",\"shortcut\":\"\"}],\"customClass\":\"f-boolean-selector\",\"tableView\":true,\"type\":\"radio\",\"key\":\"yesNo\",\"input\":true,\"defaultValue\":\"\",\"multiple\":false,\"refreshOn\":\"\",\"clearOnRefresh\":false,\"placeholder\":\"\"}],\"rules_order\":[\"Set Risk\"],\"responseTypes\":[\"yesNo\"],\"rating_mapping\":null,\"risk_mapping\":{\"rules\":[{\"operator\":\"Equals to\",\"value\":[\"no\"],\"risk\":{\"level\":\"High\",\"description\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eBy transferring more data than the absolute minimum required, you are violating the EDPB guidelines on international data transfers. By sending personal data of data subjects beyond what is necessary and adequate to jurisdictions outside of the EEA that do not have an adequacy decision (and most probably provide inadequate protections), you are opening yourself to reputational, regulatory, and investment risk.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"recommendation\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eBased on your response, you need to reduce your cross-border data transfers to only those which are essential and necessary and reduce the amount of personal data transferred to what is minimal and required for the purposes of the processing.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"owner\":1,\"deadline\":0,\"severity\":0,\"likelihood\":0,\"workflow\":null,\"dimension\":0,\"category_score\":null}}]},\"workflow_mapping\":null,\"skip_mapping\":null,\"data_map_metadata\":null}",

                    "qid": "question-1kssp543e",
                    "title": "Are you undertaking these transfers utilizing the limited exceptions/derogations provided for under Article 49 of the GDPR?",
                    "number": 1,
                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "If you are conducting transfers of personal data covered under the GDPR to non-adequate jurisdictions without the use of Article 46 transfer tools, you must ensure that these transfers fall within the limited exceptions/derogations provided for under Article 49 of the GDPR. These exceptions/derogations can only be relied upon for occasional transfers of personal data and in exceptional cases. They are as follows:\n\n*The transfer has been conducted upon the explicit consent of the Data Subject;\n*The transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract (or pre-contractual measures) between the Data Subject and Data Controller;\n*The transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract between a legal guardian of the Data Subject and Data Controller, for the benefit of the Data Subject;\n*The transfer is necessary for important reasons of public interest;\n*The transfer is necessary for the establishment or exercise of legal claims or defenses;\n*The transfer is necessary for the vital interests of the data subject - and the data subject is unable to consent;\n*The transfer is made from a register which according to Union or Member State law is intended to provide information to the public;\n*The transfer is necessary for the purposes of compelling legitimate interests pursued by the controller which are not overridden by the interests or rights and freedoms of the data subject - provided no other exception/derogation applied and the Supervisory Authority and the Data Subject are notified of the transfer.",
                    "mandatory": false,
                    "custom_builder_response": "{\"builder\":[{\"label\":\"Multiple-Choice\",\"hideLabel\":true,\"optionsLabelPosition\":\"right\",\"values\":[{\"label\":\"Yes\",\"value\":\"yes\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"Yes, but only for some transfers\",\"value\":\"yesButOnlyForSomeTransfers\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"No\",\"value\":\"no\",\"shortcut\":\"\"}],\"customClass\":\"f-compliance-selector\",\"tableView\":true,\"type\":\"radio\",\"key\":\"multipleChoice\",\"input\":true,\"defaultValue\":null,\"multiple\":false,\"refreshOn\":\"\",\"clearOnRefresh\":false,\"placeholder\":\"\"}],\"rules_order\":[],\"responseTypes\":[\"multipleChoice\"],\"rating_mapping\":null,\"risk_mapping\":null,\"workflow_mapping\":null,\"skip_mapping\":null,\"data_map_metadata\":null}",

                    "number": 2,
                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "The EDPB has provided separate guidances on the limitations on transfers under each derogation under Article 49. Please select which derogation you are relying upon.",
                    "mandatory": false,
                    "custom_builder_response": "{\"builder\":[{\"label\":\"Multi-Select\",\"hideLabel\":true,\"optionsLabelPosition\":\"right\",\"values\":[{\"label\":\"Transfer with the consent of the data subject\",\"value\":\"Choice 1\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"Transfer for fulfillment of contract in interest of or upon the request of the data subject\",\"value\":\"Choice 2\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"Transfer to pursue an important public Interest\",\"value\":\"Choice 3\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"Transfer for establishment, defense or exercise of legal claim\",\"value\":\"Choice 4\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"Transfer for the protection of vital interests of data subject\",\"value\":\"transferForTheProtectionOfVitalInterestsOfDataSubject\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"Transfer in pursuit of a compelling legitimate interest\",\"value\":\"transferInPursuitOfACompellingLegitimateInterest\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"Other\",\"value\":\"other\",\"shortcut\":\"\"}],\"customClass\":\"f-multi-selectbox\",\"tableView\":true,\"type\":\"selectboxes\",\"key\":\"multiSelect\",\"input\":true,\"defaultValue\":{\"Choice 1\":false,\"Choice 2\":false,\"Choice 3\":false,\"Choice 4\":false},\"multiple\":false,\"refreshOn\":\"\",\"clearOnRefresh\":false,\"placeholder\":\"\"}],\"rules_order\":[],\"responseTypes\":[\"multiSelect\"],\"rating_mapping\":null,\"risk_mapping\":null,\"workflow_mapping\":null,\"skip_mapping\":null,\"data_map_metadata\":null}",

                },
                {
                    "qid": "question-1ksspxs93",
                    "title": "If you are relying on the consent derogation, are you collecting data subjects' consent in accordance with EDPB requirements?",
                    "number": 3,
                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "Consent is an important derogation. You must ensure that you properly document the collection of data subjects' consent for future audits. You must also remember that as per the EDPB, consent-based transfers can only be occasional, exceptional, and strictly necessary. Finally, the consent has to be collected correctly for it to be valid, as per the EDPB's issued guidelines on 4th May 2020, consent is only valid if it is:\n\n*Freely given: it was provided without coercion and on a completely voluntary basis and the data subject is allowed to withdraw consent at any time and without any detriment;\n*Specific: it is limited for the purpose it was asked for and not for other uses of the data;\n*Informed: the data subject was made aware of all the risks and consequences of their decision to provide it;\n*Unambiguous: it has to be provided explicitly by a clear act of the data subject - ambiguous manners of the collection are not allowed.\n\nWhile transferring any special categories of data, you must ensure that the data subject has provided explicit consent. The term \"explicit\" refers to an express statement of consent, preferably in writing. In the digital context, explicit consent may be provided in the form of an electronic signature, by sending an email, by uploading a scanned document, or any other similar mechanism ensuring express and explicit consent of the data subject.",
                    "mandatory": false,
                    "custom_builder_response": "{\"builder\":[{\"label\":\"Yes/No\",\"hideLabel\":true,\"optionsLabelPosition\":\"right\",\"values\":[{\"label\":\"Yes\",\"value\":\"yes\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"No\",\"value\":\"no\",\"shortcut\":\"\"}],\"customClass\":\"f-boolean-selector\",\"tableView\":true,\"type\":\"radio\",\"key\":\"yesNo\",\"input\":true,\"defaultValue\":\"\",\"multiple\":false,\"refreshOn\":\"\",\"clearOnRefresh\":false,\"placeholder\":\"\"}],\"rules_order\":[\"Set Risk\"],\"responseTypes\":[\"yesNo\"],\"rating_mapping\":null,\"risk_mapping\":{\"rules\":[{\"operator\":\"Equals to\",\"value\":[\"no\"],\"risk\":{\"level\":\"High\",\"description\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eNot collecting data subjects consent in accordance with EDPB requirements (consent has to be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous) and relying on this derogation for international data transfers is a violation of the GDPR and opens you up to regulatory risk (fines from the Supervisory Authority which can go up to 4% of global revenues) and data subjects\\u0026#39; private right of action.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"recommendation\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eIt is recommended that you should review your consent collection techniques and bring them in line with EDPB requirements and document your consent collection comprehensively for future data audits by Supervisory Authorities before continuing to transfer data subjects\\u0026#39; data across borders.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"owner\":1,\"deadline\":0,\"severity\":0,\"likelihood\":0,\"workflow\":null,\"dimension\":0,\"category_score\":null}}]},\"workflow_mapping\":null,\"skip_mapping\":null,\"data_map_metadata\":null}",

                {
                    "qid": "question-1ksspzmy6",
                    "title": "If you are relying on the 'contractual necessity' derogation, is this data transfer necessary and limited as per EDPB requirements to fulfill a contract between you and the data subject?",
                    "number": 4,
                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "Contractual necessity is an important derogation. However, necessity requires a higher threshold than just convenience for business purposes. The necessity must arise from an objective, close and substantial connection between the data transfer and the purposes of the contract. A good rule of thumb is to consider whether the contract will be frustrated if the transfer does not take place. It’s also important to remember only occasional transfers are allowed. Transfers arising from stable business relationships which lead to repetitive transfers cannot be justified under this derogation. It would be wise to review all transfers under this derogation and note if they are occasional or repetitive and record and document reasons for the necessity for future data audits.",
                    "mandatory": false,
                    "custom_builder_response": "{\"builder\":[{\"label\":\"Yes/No\",\"hideLabel\":true,\"optionsLabelPosition\":\"right\",\"values\":[{\"label\":\"Yes\",\"value\":\"yes\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"No\",\"value\":\"no\",\"shortcut\":\"\"}],\"customClass\":\"f-boolean-selector\",\"tableView\":true,\"type\":\"radio\",\"key\":\"yesNo\",\"input\":true,\"defaultValue\":\"\",\"multiple\":false,\"refreshOn\":\"\",\"clearOnRefresh\":false,\"placeholder\":\"\"}],\"rules_order\":[\"Set Risk\"],\"responseTypes\":[\"yesNo\"],\"rating_mapping\":null,\"risk_mapping\":{\"rules\":[{\"operator\":\"Equals to\",\"value\":[\"no\"],\"risk\":{\"level\":\"High\",\"description\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eNot ensuring that all the EDPB requirements and conditions are met when transferring data internationally relying on this derogation is a violation of the GDPR and opens you up to regulatory risk (fines from the Supervisory Authority which can go up to 4% of global revenues) and data subjects\\u0026#39; private right of action.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"recommendation\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eIt is recommended that you should review all of your data transfers relying on this derogation to ensure they are necessary, limited, and follow all the EDPB requirements and conditions for the reliance on this derogation before continuing to transfer data subjects\\u0026#39; data across borders.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"owner\":1,\"deadline\":0,\"severity\":0,\"likelihood\":0,\"workflow\":null,\"dimension\":0,\"category_score\":null}}]},\"workflow_mapping\":null,\"skip_mapping\":null,\"data_map_metadata\":null}",
                    "tags": [

                {
                    "qid": "question-1kssq2esx",
                    "title": "If you are relying on \"important public interest\" derogation, is this data transfer necessary and limited as per EDPB requirements in pursuit of achieving an important public interest?",
                    "number": 5,
                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "In order to rely on the ‘important public interest’ exception for data transfers, you should be aware that as per the EDPB guidelines, such transfers are only applicable if the Union or Member State laws you are subject to recognize the public interest. It is not sufficient for such laws to only exist though. It must be apparent from the law or policy of the Union or Member State being relied upon that such transfers are possible for important public interest reasons including ‘spirit of reciprocity and ‘international cooperation'. Transfers under such derogations must be occasional and not systematic and any transfers made should be strictly limited and well documented, with all justifying material for the transfer being available for audit purposes.",
                    "mandatory": false,
                    "custom_builder_response": "{\"builder\":[{\"label\":\"Yes/No\",\"hideLabel\":true,\"optionsLabelPosition\":\"right\",\"values\":[{\"label\":\"Yes\",\"value\":\"yes\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"No\",\"value\":\"no\",\"shortcut\":\"\"}],\"customClass\":\"f-boolean-selector\",\"tableView\":true,\"type\":\"radio\",\"key\":\"yesNo\",\"input\":true,\"defaultValue\":\"\",\"multiple\":false,\"refreshOn\":\"\",\"clearOnRefresh\":false,\"placeholder\":\"\"}],\"rules_order\":[\"Set Risk\"],\"responseTypes\":[\"yesNo\"],\"rating_mapping\":null,\"risk_mapping\":{\"rules\":[{\"operator\":\"Equals to\",\"value\":[\"no\"],\"risk\":{\"level\":\"High\",\"description\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eNot ensuring that all the EDPB requirements and conditions are met when transferring data internationally relying on this derogation is a violation of the GDPR and opens you up to regulatory risk (fines from the Supervisory Authority which can go up to 4% of global revenues) and data subjects\\u0026#39; private right of action.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"recommendation\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eIt is recommended that you should review all of your data transfers relying on this derogation to ensure they are necessary, limited, and follow all the EDPB requirements and conditions for the reliance on this derogation before continuing to transfer data subjects\\u0026#39; data across borders.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"owner\":1,\"deadline\":0,\"severity\":0,\"likelihood\":0,\"workflow\":null,\"dimension\":0,\"category_score\":null}}]},\"workflow_mapping\":null,\"skip_mapping\":null,\"data_map_metadata\":null}",

                {
                    "qid": "question-1kssq58ek",
                    "title": "If you are relying on \"establishment, exercise or defence of a legal claim\" derogation, is this data transfer necessary and limited as per EDPB requirements in pursuit of establishing, exercising, or defense of a legal claim?",
                    "number": 6,
                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "In order to rely on ‘establishment, defense or exercise of legal claims’ derogation, you must ensure that data transfers are occasional and necessary in relation to a contract or a legal claim.                     "number": 1,
                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "The EDPB requires that data exporters, with the aid of data importers, analyze the laws/regulations/practices of the recipient jurisdiction to assess the effectiveness of the protections provided to the transferred data by the Article 46 transfer tool. It is expected that data exporters must ensure that Article 46 tools are not just paper protections to the transferred data - they should be enforceable and practically implementable protections in the recipient jurisdiction. The standard for the protection of the transferred data has to be 'essentially equivalent to the protections provided to the personal data in the EU (through the GDPR). Focus on laws and practices which would apply to the transferred data, the data importer, and would impinge the effectiveness of the safeguards contained in the Article 46 transfer tool in particular. You should document the process. It is important to note that the scope of your assessment is limited to the legislation and practices relevant to the protection of the specific data you transfer. \n\nThe following things need to be considered to conduct a holistic assessment:\n\n*Scale and regularity of transfers;\n*Length of the processing chain;\n*Number of actors involved and the transmission channels used; \n*Purposes for which the data are transferred and processed;\n*Types of entities involved in the processing; \n*Sector/Industry in which the transfer occurs (and any sector-specific laws/regulations/practices);\n*Categories of personal data transferred; \n*Whether the data will be stored in the recipient jurisdiction or whether there is only remote access to data stored within the EU/EEA;\n*Format of the data to be transferred; \n*Possibility that the data may be subject to onward transfers to another jurisdiction;\n*Past experiences transferring to the recipient jurisdiction (whether any data access requests by public authorities of the recipient country have ever been received);\n*Rule of law situation in the recipient jurisdiction;\n*Existence of a comprehensive data protection law or an independent data protection authority (or sectoral specific if applicable) in the recipient jurisdiction;\n*Adherence to international instruments providing for data protection safeguards by the recipient jurisdiction.\n* If the data importer’s commitments enabling DSR requests as provided in the Article 46 GDPR transfer tool (such as access, correction, and deletion requests for transferred data, as well as (judicial) redress) can be effectively applied in practice under the law of the recipient jurisdiction.\n*Sources of information on the basis of which you assess the law and practice of the recipient jurisdiction.\n\nYou must ensure the information you rely on is relevant, objective, reliable, verifiable, and accessible.                     "number": 2,
                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "EDPB requires that data exporters must focus particularly on surveillance laws and practices of recipient jurisdictions which allow public authorities in the recipient jurisdiction to surveil/access/acquire the transferred personal data. If these essential guarantees are not respected by the laws and practices allowing public authorities to surveil the transferred data, then this interference has to be considered unjustifiable and a violation of the safeguards provided to the personal data by the Article 46 transfer tool. It is important that the primary focus of the analysis should be surveillance laws (and other laws and regulations providing public authorities similar powers in relation to the transferred personal data). However, in case there are no laws on public surveillance in the recipient jurisdiction (or they are not publically available), other objective factors can be relied upon such as known practices, reported precedents, legislation, established practices as well as technical, financial, and human resources of the recipient jurisdiction's public authorities in being able to intercept communications of the transferred data and being able to overcome technical protections (i.e encryption, etc.) It is also important to note that while the laws of the recipient jurisdiction might guarantee EU essential guarantees, the practices of public authorities may clearly indicate that they do not normally apply/comply with the legislation that governs their activities. The following factors must be focused upon as per the EDPB guidance on EU essential guarantees:\n\n*Legal basis: Interference/surveillance must be based on clear, precise, foreseeable, and accessible rules contained in legally binding domestic law in the recipient country.\n\n*Necessity and proportionality: Interference/surveillance must be strictly necessary and proportional to the objectives/aims pursued by the public authorities of the recipient jurisdiction (the interference/surveillance must not be general or bulk in nature and must define the scope of the interference).\n\n*Independent oversight mechanisms: There must be an independent and impartial mechanism (such as a judge) to oversee the implementation of surveillance measures in the third country to reduce arbitrariness and abuse.\n\n*Effective remedies for data subjects: There must be effective remedies available within the law for a data subject to exercise their rights and seek redress when public authorities do not comply with the domestic laws or rules on public surveillance - this is linked with the right of data subject to be notified of the interference. An independent authority such as a judicial authority must be entrusted with listening to Data Subjects' redressal requests and must have the power to remedy non-compliance by public authorities and enforce data subjects' rights.\n\n*Analysis of practices of public authorities, if there are no surveillance laws or rules (or publicly available laws or rules) or the laws, are not followed by the public authorities in practice.\n\nSignificant consideration must be made to supplementary measures where an assessment results that the third country does not meet the above-mentioned minimum Essential Guarantees.",

                {
                    "qid": "question-1kssr0uvx",
                    "title": "Does the recipient jurisdiction provide an essentially equivalent level of protection to the transferred data and make the safeguards employed for the protection of the transferred data under the Article 46 tool implementable and effective?",
                    "number": 3,
                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "The EDPB requires that data exporters with the assistance of data importers assess the laws and practices of the recipient jurisdiction so as to confirm if the appropriate safeguards for the transferred data under the Article 46 transfer tool are implementable and effective measures and thus the level of protection for the transferred data is 'essentially equivalent'. This process should be documented and if any gaps are identified, they should be addressed with 'supplementary measures'. It should be noted:\n\n*The appropriate safeguards contained in the Article 46 tool must be implementable and effective (i.e if the law of the recipient jurisdiction prohibits a practice or enforceability of the SCCs against the data importer, then those protections must be deemed unimplementable and ineffective);\n\n*Since SCCs and BCRs (and most of the other Article 46 transfer tools) are private agreements (i.e contractual guarantees) between two private parties, surveillance laws or practices providing public authorities access to the transferred data can overcome the safeguards contained therein;\n\n*If surveillance laws or practices in the recipient country that provide public authorities powers to surveil/access/acquire the transferred data are not violative of the EDPB's guidance on EU essential guarantees, they are not violative of the 'essentially equivalent' level of protection provided to the data by the safeguards contained in the Article 46 transfer tool;\n\n*However, if the surveillance laws and practices of the recipient country are violative of EDPB's guidance on EU essential guarantees, then the protections afforded to the transferred personal data by the Article 46 transfer tools might be unimplementable or ineffective;",
                    "mandatory": false,
                    "custom_builder_response": "{\"builder\":[{\"label\":\"Yes/No\",\"hideLabel\":true,\"optionsLabelPosition\":\"right\",\"values\":[{\"label\":\"Yes\",\"value\":\"yes\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"No\",\"value\":\"no\",\"shortcut\":\"\"}],\"customClass\":\"f-boolean-selector\",\"tableView\":true,\"type\":\"radio\",\"key\":\"yesNo\",\"input\":true,\"defaultValue\":\"\",\"multiple\":false,\"refreshOn\":\"\",\"clearOnRefresh\":false,\"placeholder\":\"\"}],\"rules_order\":[\"Set Risk\"],\"responseTypes\":[\"yesNo\"],\"rating_mapping\":null,\"risk_mapping\":{\"rules\":[{\"operator\":\"Equals to\",\"value\":[\"no\"],\"risk\":{\"level\":\"High\",\"description\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eIf the recipient jurisdiction\\u0026#39;s laws or practices make the safeguards for the transferred personal data contained in the Article 46 transfer tool unimplementable or ineffective or the surveillance laws or practices that authorize public authorities to surveil/access/acquire the transferred personal data do not meet the standards of EDPB\\u0026#39;s guidance on EU essential guarantees, then the transferred personal data is no longer provided an \\u0026#39;essentially equivalent\\u0026#39; level of protection and thus data subject\\u0026#39;s rights under the GDPR are threatened and at risk.             "heading": "Supplementary Measures",
            "number": 5,
            "category": "",
            "questions": [
                {
                    "qid": "question-1kssr5t1g",
                    "title": "Are you taking or can you take supplementary measures to protect the transferred personal data and ensure it receives an 'essentially equivalent' level of protection in the recipient jurisdiction?",
                    "number": 1,
                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "The EDPB in its most recent guidance on international data transfers has recommended data exporters to ensure supplementary measures (technical measures supplemented by contractual and organizational measures) are implemented when the legal analysis of a non-EEA recipient jurisdiction (with no adequacy decision) reveals that the safeguards for the data transferred under the Article 46 tool are unimplementable or ineffective especially if this is due to surveillance laws or practices, which provide the recipient jurisdiction's public authorities the power to surveil/access/acquire the transferred personal data in excess of the standards established by EDPB's guidance on EU essential guarantees. However, you may decide to proceed with the transfer without being required to implement supplementary measures, if you consider that you have no reason to believe that relevant and problematic legislation identified by your assessment will be applied, in practice, to your transferred data and/or importer. It is important to note that to take advantage of this exemption, you must prepare a detailed report to show that the guarantees provided by the Article 46 transfer tool shall not be impugned by the problematic legislation since they do not apply in practice to the transferred data or importer.                     "title": "Have you employed or are you employing encryption to the transferred data in a manner that makes it an effective supplementary measure as per the EDPB?",
                    "number": 3,
                    "description": "",
                    "additional_details": "In its most recent guidance on international transfers, the EDPB has stressed on technical measures as the most important supplementary measures (supplemented by contractual or organizational measures) to protect the transferred data. For encryption, several conditional factors need to be considered, specifically the two points when the recipient jurisdiction's public authorities might try to surveil/access/acquire the personal information: during transit or when at rest. Thus, encryption must protect the data at both points. It is also important to note that the encryption must not be banned or made illegal by the law of the recipient jurisdiction (or mandate backdoors to be created for public authorities). The EDPB has not specified any checklist of factors that can ensure that encryption is an effective supplementary measure but in footnote 80 of its most recent guidance has stated 'data exporters can rely on technical guidance published by official cybersecurity authorities of the EU and its member states and from examples of use cases the following factors which should be considered can be inferred:\n\n*Strong encryption before transmission;\n*Encryption algorithm and its parameterization considered robust against third country’s cryptanalysis capabilities;\n*Strength of the encryption takes into account the amount of time personal data is to be kept safe (The protective capacity of cryptographic algorithms is subject to decline over time due to the discovery of new cryptanalytic techniques - thus with time the protection offered by an obsolete encryption technique degrades);\n*Encryption algorithm is flawlessly implemented (proper software, certification);\n*Encryption keys reliably managed;\n*Encryption keys are retained by data exporter or a third party based in EEA or an organization in a third country considered adequate;\n*Encryption methodology is updated as per technological updates and constantly monitored;\n*Transport encryption is used (when it is in transit);\n*Decryption is only possible outside the recipient jurisdiction (when being routed from the recipient jurisdiction to another adequate jurisdiction);\n*Use of a trustworthy public-key certification authority or infrastructure (when being routed from the recipient jurisdiction to another adequate jurisdiction);\n*Specific protective and state-of-the-art measures against active and passive attacks employed (when being routed or in transit);\n*Use end-to-end encryption if transport encryption is believed to be compromised (when being routed or in transit);\n*No backdoors must exist in the software or hardware.",

By sending personal data of data subjects beyond what is necessary and adequate to jurisdictions outside of the EEA that do not have an adequacy decision (and most probably provide inadequate protections), you are opening yourself to reputational, regulatory, and investment risk.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"recommendation\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eBased on your response, you need to reduce your cross-border data transfers to only those which are essential and necessary and reduce the amount of personal data transferred to what is minimal and required for the purposes of the processing.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"owner\":1,\"deadline\":0,\"severity\":0,\"likelihood\":0,\"workflow\":null,\"dimension\":0,\"category_score\":null}}]},\"workflow_mapping\":null,\"skip_mapping\":null,\"data_map_metadata\":null}",

                            "additional_details": "If you are conducting transfers of personal data covered under the GDPR to non-adequate jurisdictions without the use of Article 46 transfer tools, you must ensure that these transfers fall within the limited exceptions/derogations provided for under Article 49 of the GDPR. These exceptions/derogations can only be relied upon for occasional transfers of personal data and in exceptional cases. They are as follows:\n\n*The transfer has been conducted upon the explicit consent of the Data Subject;\n*The transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract (or pre-contractual measures) between the Data Subject and Data Controller;\n*The transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract between a legal guardian of the Data Subject and Data Controller, for the benefit of the Data Subject;\n*The transfer is necessary for important reasons of public interest;\n*The transfer is necessary for the establishment or exercise of legal claims or defenses;\n*The transfer is necessary for the vital interests of the data subject - and the data subject is unable to consent;\n*The transfer is made from a register which according to Union or Member State law is intended to provide information to the public;\n*The transfer is necessary for the purposes of compelling legitimate interests pursued by the controller which are not overridden by the interests or rights and freedoms of the data subject - provided no other exception/derogation applied and the Supervisory Authority and the Data Subject are notified of the transfer.",

                            "additional_details": "Consent is an important derogation. You must ensure that you properly document the collection of data subjects' consent for future audits. You must also remember that as per the EDPB, consent-based transfers can only be occasional, exceptional, and strictly necessary. Finally, the consent has to be collected correctly for it to be valid, as per the EDPB's issued guidelines on 4th May 2020, consent is only valid if it is:\n\n*Freely given: it was provided without coercion and on a completely voluntary basis and the data subject is allowed to withdraw consent at any time and without any detriment;\n*Specific: it is limited for the purpose it was asked for and not for other uses of the data;\n*Informed: the data subject was made aware of all the risks and consequences of their decision to provide it;\n*Unambiguous: it has to be provided explicitly by a clear act of the data subject - ambiguous manners of the collection are not allowed.\n\nWhile transferring any special categories of data, you must ensure that the data subject has provided explicit consent. The term \"explicit\" refers to an express statement of consent, preferably in writing.                             "mandatory": false,

It would be wise to review all transfers under this derogation and note if they are occasional or repetitive and record and document reasons for the necessity for future data audits.",
                            "mandatory": false,

                        {
                            "qid": "question-1kssq8tqd",
                            "title": "If you are relying on \"protection of vital interest of the data subject\" derogation, is this data transfer necessary and limited as per EDPB requirements for protecting the vital interests of the data subject, provided that the data subject is physically or legally incapacitated to give consent?",
                            "number": 7,
                            "description": "",
                            "additional_details": "To make transfers ‘for the data subject’s vital interests’ when they do not possess the 'mental or legal capacity' you must ensure that the data subject has a medical emergency or any other such situation which reaches the required threshold where the imminent risk of serious harm to the data subject outweighs data protection concerns. You must also ensure the data being sent is necessary to reduce or mitigate the risk of serious harm to the data subject i.e if it is a medical emergency only data required to treat the data subject can be sent. Lastly, it is important to ensure the data subject is mentally or legally incapacitated to give consent. If they are not, then consent needs to be taken regardless of the risk of harm. If you are transferring data under this derogation you must document all the reasons and justifications diligently along with all supporting evidence (especially related to the data subject’s physical or mental incapacity which might require a medical or legal opinion from a relevant professional) for data audit purposes.",

                        {
                            "qid": "question-1kssqajyh",
                            "title": "If you are relying on \"compelling legitimate interest\" derogation, is the data transfer necessary and limited as per EDPB requirements for the purposes of pursuing a compelling legitimate interest?",
                            "number": 8,
                            "description": "",
                            "additional_details": "For transfers of data made by you for pursuing ‘compelling legitimate interests’ it is necessary that you take into account all factors, especially the risk of harm to the data subject, and balance them with the legitimate interests you are pursuing. The important factors that need to be accounted for by you in this balancing exercise to take advantage of this derogation are:\n\n*The EDPB sees this as a measure of last resort. It must be shown by you that none of the safeguards were a viable option for this data transfer and none of the other derogations could be reasonably relied upon to make this data transfer;\n*Particular consideration to the nature of the personal data, the purpose and duration of the proposed processing operation or operations, as well as the situation in the country of origin, the third country, and the country of final destination needs to be taken by you; \n*A higher threshold is required as your legitimate interests need to be ‘compelling’ i.e they must be requiring urgent attention or there might be a high risk of loss or harm to you (personal, financial, reputational, etc.);\n*Transfers under this derogation cannot be repetitive - they must be exceptional;\n*Transfers cannot be on a large scale i.e transfer must be limited to the data of just those data subjects whose data needs to be transferred necessarily;\n*The data subject and relevant data protection authority need to be informed of the transfer. \n*Any risks to the data subjects found in the balancing exercise conducted by you must be mandatorily addressed by employing additional safeguards to mitigate the risk of harm to the data subject.",

                            "qid": "question-1kssqqipe",
                            "title": "Have you undertaken a legal assessment of the recipient jurisdiction to assess the effectiveness of the safeguards by Article 46 transfer tool to protect the transferred personal data?",
                            "number": 1,
                            "description": "",
                            "additional_details": "The EDPB requires that data exporters, with the aid of data importers, analyze the laws/regulations/practices of the recipient jurisdiction to assess the effectiveness of the protections provided to the transferred data by the Article 46 transfer tool. It is expected that data exporters must ensure that Article 46 tools are not just paper protections to the transferred data - they should be enforceable and practically implementable protections in the recipient jurisdiction. The standard for the protection of the transferred data has to be 'essentially equivalent to the protections provided to the personal data in the EU (through the GDPR). Focus on laws and practices which would apply to the transferred data, the data importer, and would impinge the effectiveness of the safeguards contained in the Article 46 transfer tool in particular. You should document the process. It is important to note that the scope of your assessment is limited to the legislation and practices relevant to the protection of the specific data you transfer. \n\nThe following things need to be considered to conduct a holistic assessment:\n\n*Scale and regularity of transfers;\n*Length of the processing chain;\n*Number of actors involved and the transmission channels used; \n*Purposes for which the data are transferred and processed;\n*Types of entities involved in the processing; \n*Sector/Industry in which the transfer occurs (and any sector-specific laws/regulations/practices);\n*Categories of personal data transferred; \n*Whether the data will be stored in the recipient jurisdiction or whether there is only remote access to data stored within the EU/EEA;\n*Format of the data to be transferred; \n*Possibility that the data may be subject to onward transfers to another jurisdiction;\n*Past experiences transferring to the recipient jurisdiction (whether any data access requests by public authorities of the recipient country have ever been received);\n*Rule of law situation in the recipient jurisdiction;\n*Existence of a comprehensive data protection law or an independent data protection authority (or sectoral specific if applicable) in the recipient jurisdiction;\n*Adherence to international instruments providing for data protection safeguards by the recipient jurisdiction.\n* If the data importer’s commitments enabling DSR requests as provided in the Article 46 GDPR transfer tool (such as access, correction, and deletion requests for transferred data, as well as (judicial) redress) can be effectively applied in practice under the law of the recipient jurisdiction.\n*Sources of information on the basis of which you assess the law and practice of the recipient jurisdiction.\n\nYou must ensure the information you rely on is relevant, objective, reliable, verifiable, and accessible.  You can even take into account the experience of other actors operating within the same sector and/or related to similar transferred personal data and documented practical experience of the importer with\nrelevant prior instances of requests for access received from public authorities in the third country as an additional source of information. For more information on which sources you can rely on, you should refer to paragraphs 44-47 and Annex 3 of the EDPB's latest recommendations on supplementary safeguards for cross-border transfer.",

                            "qid": "question-1kssqw8mo",
                            "title": "Have you analyzed the surveillance laws and practices of the recipient jurisdiction (i.e laws that allow surveillance/access/acquisition of data by public authorities) in the legal analysis mentioned above?",
                            "number": 2,
                            "description": "",
                            "additional_details": "EDPB requires that data exporters must focus particularly on surveillance laws and practices of recipient jurisdictions which allow public authorities in the recipient jurisdiction to surveil/access/acquire the transferred personal data. For the purposes of these laws, data exporters must focus on EDPB's guidance on EU essential guarantees to see whether these laws and practices conform with these guarantees. If these essential guarantees are not respected by the laws and practices allowing public authorities to surveil the transferred data, then this interference has to be considered unjustifiable and a violation of the safeguards provided to the personal data by the Article 46 transfer tool. It is important that the primary focus of the analysis should be surveillance laws (and other laws and regulations providing public authorities similar powers in relation to the transferred personal data). However, in case there are no laws on public surveillance in the recipient jurisdiction (or they are not publically available), other objective factors can be relied upon such as known practices, reported precedents, legislation, established practices as well as technical, financial, and human resources of the recipient jurisdiction's public authorities in being able to intercept communications of the transferred data and being able to overcome technical protections (i.e encryption, etc.) It is also important to note that while the laws of the recipient jurisdiction might guarantee EU essential guarantees, the practices of public authorities may clearly indicate that they do not normally apply/comply with the legislation that governs their activities. The following factors must be focused upon as per the EDPB guidance on EU essential guarantees:\n\n*Legal basis: Interference/surveillance must be based on clear, precise, foreseeable, and accessible rules contained in legally binding domestic law in the recipient country.\n\n*Necessity and proportionality: Interference/surveillance must be strictly necessary and proportional to the objectives/aims pursued by the public authorities of the recipient jurisdiction (the interference/surveillance must not be general or bulk in nature and must define the scope of the interference).\n\n*Independent oversight mechanisms: There must be an independent and impartial mechanism (such as a judge) to oversee the implementation of surveillance measures in the third country to reduce arbitrariness and abuse.\n\n*Effective remedies for data subjects: There must be effective remedies available within the law for a data subject to exercise their rights and seek redress when public authorities do not comply with the domestic laws or rules on public surveillance - this is linked with the right of data subject to be notified of the interference. An independent authority such as a judicial authority must be entrusted with listening to Data Subjects' redressal requests and must have the power to remedy non-compliance by public authorities and enforce data subjects' rights.\n\n*Analysis of practices of public authorities, if there are no surveillance laws or rules (or publicly available laws or rules) or the laws, are not followed by the public authorities in practice.\n\nSignificant consideration must be made to supplementary measures where an assessment results that the third country does not meet the above-mentioned minimum Essential Guarantees.",

If this analysis is not undertaken, it risks opening you up to regulatory risks as the relevant Supervisory Authorities may ask for a record of this assessment and its result during a future audit and may order the suspension of the data transfer and impose fines if it is discovered you have no taken this activity as different \\u0026#39;inadequate\\u0026#39; non-EEA jurisdictions may have laws and practices which nullify the protections provided to the transferred personal data by the Article 46 tool - a fact that will not be discovered unless this legal analysis is undertaken.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"recommendation\":\"\\u003cp\\u003ePlease conduct a comprehensive legal analysis of the recipient jurisdiction to identify surveillance laws and practices that are unjustifiable and undermine the protections provided by the Article 46 transfer tool utilized to provide an \\u0026#39;essentially equivalent\\u0026#39; level of protection to the transferred personal data and the EDPB\\u0026#39;s guidance on EU Essential Guarantees. Document this process and its results.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"owner\":1,\"deadline\":0,\"severity\":0,\"likelihood\":0,\"workflow\":null,\"dimension\":0,\"category_score\":null}}]},\"workflow_mapping\":null,\"skip_mapping\":null,\"data_map_metadata\":null}",

                        {
                            "qid": "question-1kssr0uvx",
                            "title": "Does the recipient jurisdiction provide an essentially equivalent level of protection to the transferred data and make the safeguards employed for the protection of the transferred data under the Article 46 tool implementable and effective?",
                            "number": 3,
                            "description": "",
                            "additional_details": "The EDPB requires that data exporters with the assistance of data importers assess the laws and practices of the recipient jurisdiction so as to confirm if the appropriate safeguards for the transferred data under the Article 46 transfer tool are implementable and effective measures and thus the level of protection for the transferred data is 'essentially equivalent'. This process should be documented and if any gaps are identified, they should be addressed with 'supplementary measures'. It should be noted:\n\n*The appropriate safeguards contained in the Article 46 tool must be implementable and effective (i.e if the law of the recipient jurisdiction prohibits a practice or enforceability of the SCCs against the data importer, then those protections must be deemed unimplementable and ineffective);\n\n*Since SCCs and BCRs (and most of the other Article 46 transfer tools) are private agreements (i.e contractual guarantees) between two private parties, surveillance laws or practices providing public authorities access to the transferred data can overcome the safeguards contained therein;\n\n*If surveillance laws or practices in the recipient country that provide public authorities powers to surveil/access/acquire the transferred data are not violative of the EDPB's guidance on EU essential guarantees, they are not violative of the 'essentially equivalent' level of protection provided to the data by the safeguards contained in the Article 46 transfer tool;\n\n*However, if the surveillance laws and practices of the recipient country are violative of EDPB's guidance on EU essential guarantees, then the protections afforded to the transferred personal data by the Article 46 transfer tools might be unimplementable or ineffective;",
                            "mandatory": false,
                            "custom_builder_response": "{\"builder\":[{\"label\":\"Yes/No\",\"hideLabel\":true,\"optionsLabelPosition\":\"right\",\"values\":[{\"label\":\"Yes\",\"value\":\"yes\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"No\",\"value\":\"no\",\"shortcut\":\"\"}],\"customClass\":\"f-boolean-selector\",\"tableView\":true,\"type\":\"radio\",\"key\":\"yesNo\",\"input\":true,\"defaultValue\":\"\",\"multiple\":false,\"refreshOn\":\"\",\"clearOnRefresh\":false,\"placeholder\":\"\"}],\"rules_order\":[\"Set Risk\"],\"responseTypes\":[\"yesNo\"],\"rating_mapping\":null,\"risk_mapping\":{\"rules\":[{\"operator\":\"Equals to\",\"value\":[\"no\"],\"risk\":{\"level\":\"High\",\"description\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eIf the recipient jurisdiction\\u0026#39;s laws or practices make the safeguards for the transferred personal data contained in the Article 46 transfer tool unimplementable or ineffective or the surveillance laws or practices that authorize public authorities to surveil/access/acquire the transferred personal data do not meet the standards of EDPB\\u0026#39;s guidance on EU essential guarantees, then the transferred personal data is no longer provided an \\u0026#39;essentially equivalent\\u0026#39; level of protection and thus data subject\\u0026#39;s rights under the GDPR are threatened and at risk. If this risk goes unaddressed it opens you up to regulatory risk (fines up to 4% of global revenues and bans on further transfers). Thus it is important to address this risk by employing \\u0026#39;supplementary measures\\u0026#39;.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"recommendation\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eIt is important that you undertake \\u0026#39;supplementary measures\\u0026#39; to further protect the personal data to overcome the gaps recognized in your legal assessment of the recipient jurisdiction\\u0026#39;s legal system and surveillance practices.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"owner\":1,\"deadline\":0,\"severity\":0,\"likelihood\":0,\"workflow\":null,\"dimension\":0,\"category_score\":null}}]},\"workflow_mapping\":null,\"skip_mapping\":null,\"data_map_metadata\":null}",

                {
                    "id": 0,
                    "heading": "Supplementary Measures",
                    "number": 5,
                    "category": "",
                    "questions": [
                        {
                            "qid": "question-1kssr5t1g",
                            "title": "Are you taking or can you take supplementary measures to protect the transferred personal data and ensure it receives an 'essentially equivalent' level of protection in the recipient jurisdiction?",
                            "number": 1,
                            "description": "",
                            "additional_details": "The EDPB in its most recent guidance on international data transfers has recommended data exporters to ensure supplementary measures (technical measures supplemented by contractual and organizational measures) are implemented when the legal analysis of a non-EEA recipient jurisdiction (with no adequacy decision) reveals that the safeguards for the data transferred under the Article 46 tool are unimplementable or ineffective especially if this is due to surveillance laws or practices, which provide the recipient jurisdiction's public authorities the power to surveil/access/acquire the transferred personal data in excess of the standards established by EDPB's guidance on EU essential guarantees. However, you may decide to proceed with the transfer without being required to implement supplementary measures, if you consider that you have no reason to believe that relevant and problematic legislation identified by your assessment will be applied, in practice, to your transferred data and/or importer. It is important to note that to take advantage of this exemption, you must prepare a detailed report to show that the guarantees provided by the Article 46 transfer tool shall not be impugned by the problematic legislation since they do not apply in practice to the transferred data or importer. However, the report does not exempt you from providing for the necessary supplementary measures (e.g. end-to-end encryption of data) to protect personal data during its transmission and processing in the recipient jurisdiction if your analysis of the applicable legislation of the recipient jurisdiction indicates that access to data may also take place, even in the absence of the importer’s intervention at this moment of transfer.\n\nEach supplementary measure should also be assessed under which conditions it would be effective in covering the gaps or deficiencies in the legal setup of the recipient jurisdiction which threaten the transferred data. It should be carefully examined whether the supplementary measures can be taken (are there any laws which prohibit the implementation or enforcement of the supplementary measures), whether they shall be effective (do they address the gap or deficiency completely and in the different and various ways the data can be surveilled/accessed/acquired by public authorities) and whether the data importer shall implement them. Some of the data planned for transfer may require supplementary measures whereas other data may not (considering formal and/or practical application of the recipient jurisdiction's law). Factors companies must account for in implementing supplementary measures are the following (non-exhaustive):\n\n*Format of the data to be transferred (i.e. in plain text/pseudonymized or encrypted); \n*Nature of the data (e.g. a higher level of protection is afforded in the EEA to categories of data covered by articles 9 and 10 GDPR);\n*Length and complexity of data processing workflow;\n*Number of actors involved in the processing, and their relationship;\n*Possibility that the data may be subject to onward transfers, within the same or even to another third country.",
                            "mandatory": false,

                            "number": 2,
                            "description": "",
                            "additional_details": "As per the EDPB's recent guidance if the data exporter reasonably believes that problematic legislations, in the recipient jurisdiction, identified through the assessment shall not be applied, in practice, to the transferred data and/or importer, thus not affecting the safeguards implemented within the Article 46 transfer tool, the data exporter may choose not to implement supplementary measures and may choose to proceed with the transfer. Reports should be endorsed by the legal representative of the exporter and shall take into account:\n*Comprehensive information on the legal assessment of the legislation and practices, and of their application to the specific transfers;\n*The internal procedure to produce the assessment (including information on actors involved in the assessment-e.g. law firms, consultants, or internal departments, etc.) and dates of the checks;\n*The experience of other actors operating within the same sector and/or related to similar transferred personal data;\n*Other sources of information specified in Annex 3 of the EDPB's final recommendations on supplementary measures for cross-border transfer of data.\n\nIf the data exporter cannot implement supplementary measures to provide an 'essentially equivalent' level of protection to the transferred data, the data importer should be made to delete or return all the previously transferred data and all present and future data transfers to the recipient jurisdiction should be immediately suspended unless supplementary measures can be implemented (or are implemented). The EDPB requires that the deletion or return of previously transferred data and the suspension of all present and future transfers to the recipient jurisdiction should be recorded and documented for future data audits.                         {
                            "qid": "question-1kssrz0ye",
                            "title": "Have you employed or are you employing encryption to the transferred data in a manner that makes it an effective supplementary measure as per the EDPB?",
                            "number": 3,
                            "description": "",
                            "additional_details": "In its most recent guidance on international transfers, the EDPB has stressed on technical measures as the most important supplementary measures (supplemented by contractual or organizational measures) to protect the transferred data. For encryption, several conditional factors need to be considered, specifically the two points when the recipient jurisdiction's public authorities might try to surveil/access/acquire the personal information: during transit or when at rest. Thus, encryption must protect the data at both points. It is also important to note that the encryption must not be banned or made illegal by the law of the recipient jurisdiction (or mandate backdoors to be created for public authorities). The EDPB has not specified any checklist of factors that can ensure that encryption is an effective supplementary measure but in footnote 80 of its most recent guidance has stated 'data exporters can rely on technical guidance published by official cybersecurity authorities of the EU and its member states and from examples of use cases the following factors which should be considered can be inferred:\n\n*Strong encryption before transmission;\n*Encryption algorithm and its parameterization considered robust against third country’s cryptanalysis capabilities;\n*Strength of the encryption takes into account the amount of time personal data is to be kept safe (The protective capacity of cryptographic algorithms is subject to decline over time due to the discovery of new cryptanalytic techniques - thus with time the protection offered by an obsolete encryption technique degrades);\n*Encryption algorithm is flawlessly implemented (proper software, certification);\n*Encryption keys reliably managed;\n*Encryption keys are retained by data exporter or a third party based in EEA or an organization in a third country considered adequate;\n*Encryption methodology is updated as per technological updates and constantly monitored;\n*Transport encryption is used (when it is in transit);\n*Decryption is only possible outside the recipient jurisdiction (when being routed from the recipient jurisdiction to another adequate jurisdiction);\n*Use of a trustworthy public-key certification authority or infrastructure (when being routed from the recipient jurisdiction to another adequate jurisdiction);\n*Specific protective and state-of-the-art measures against active and passive attacks employed (when being routed or in transit);\n*Use end-to-end encryption if transport encryption is believed to be compromised (when being routed or in transit);\n*No backdoors must exist in the software or hardware.",
                            "mandatory": false,
                            "custom_builder_response": "{\"builder\":[{\"label\":\"Yes/No\",\"hideLabel\":true,\"optionsLabelPosition\":\"right\",\"values\":[{\"label\":\"Yes\",\"value\":\"yes\",\"shortcut\":\"\"},{\"label\":\"No\",\"value\":\"no\",\"shortcut\":\"\"}],\"customClass\":\"f-boolean-selector\",\"tableView\":true,\"type\":\"radio\",\"key\":\"yesNo\",\"input\":true,\"defaultValue\":\"\",\"multiple\":false,\"refreshOn\":\"\",\"clearOnRefresh\":false,\"placeholder\":\"\"}],\"rules_order\":[\"Set Risk\"],\"responseTypes\":[\"yesNo\"],\"rating_mapping\":null,\"risk_mapping\":{\"rules\":[{\"operator\":\"Equals to\",\"value\":[\"no\"],\"risk\":{\"level\":\"High\",\"description\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eIf the transferred personal data is not encrypted or is not encrypted in a manner that is effective in protecting it, it allows for it to be intercepted and accessible by third parties (most notably, public authorities in recipient jurisdictions). This poses risks for the data subjects and makes you liable for the violation of the GDPR, which can make you liable to regulatory risks (penalties that can go up to 4% of your global revenues and suspensions of international transfers of data) as well data subjects\\u0026#39; private rights of actions.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"recommendation\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eIf you are not employing encryption, in transit or at rest, for the transferred personal data, you should immediately undertake it. If your encryption methods and mechanisms are not up to par with the risk posed to the transferred data, the cryptography capabilities of the public authorities of the recipient jurisdiction, the context of the data transfer, technological updates, and/or EDPB\\u0026#39;s guidelines, they must be immediately updated. If encryption cannot be implemented up to those standards, other technical measures (supplemented by contractual and organizational measures) should be undertaken.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"owner\":1,\"deadline\":0,\"severity\":0,\"likelihood\":0,\"workflow\":null,\"dimension\":0,\"category_score\":null}}]},\"workflow_mapping\":null,\"skip_mapping\":null,\"data_map_metadata\":null}",

                            "title": "Have you pseudonymized or are you pseudonymizing the transferred data in a manner that makes it an effective supplementary measure as per the EDPB?",
                            "number": 4,
                            "description": "",
                            "additional_details": "In its most recent guidance on international transfers, the EDPB has stressed on technical measures as the most important supplementary measures (supplemented by contractual or organizational measures) to protect the transferred data. Several conditional factors need to be considered, which are listed below (non-exhaustive):\n\n*The data cannot be used anymore in any manner to re-identify the data subject without additional information;\n*The additional information is retained by data exporter or a third party based in EEA or an organization in a third country considered adequate;\n*Additional information and means of reidentifying the data adequately protected by safeguards (Additional data may consist of tables juxtaposing pseudonyms with the identifying attributes they replace, cryptographic keys or other parameters for the transformation of attributes, or other data permitting the attribution of the pseudonymized data to identified or identifiable natural persons);\n*An analysis confirms that public authorities of the recipient jurisdiction cannot reidentify the data even if cross-referenced with other data they might possess.",

This would invite unneeded risk to data subjects\\u0026#39; as their data and their identities would become available to a third party interceptor (including public authorities of the recipient jurisdiction). This would make you liable for a violation of the GDPR and can open you up to regulatory risks (4% of global revenues and suspension of international data transfers) along with data subjects\\u0026#39; private right of action.\\u003c/p\\u003e\",\"recommendation\":\"\\u003cp\\u003eIf you are transferring personal data to a recipient jurisdiction outside of the EEA area, which does not have an adequacy decision and has a legal system that cannot guarantee the effectiveness of protections provided to the data under the employed Article 46 transfer tool (especially due to public surveillance laws which do not match the standards of EDPB\\u0026#39;s guidance on EU essential guarantees), for the purposes of statistical or trend analysis, then it is recommended you pseudonymize the data to remove identifying information, thus ensuring data subjects\\u0026#39; privacy rights are not violated if the data is intercepted.                             "number": 8,
                            "description": "",
                            "additional_details": "As per the EDPB's latest guidance on international data transfers, the EDPB has suggested that contractual measures should be put in place to supplement the technical measures and legally obligate the data importer to take steps to protect the data. Thus data importers can be obligated to:\n*Disclose and enumerate to the data exporter the laws, regulations, and practices in the recipient jurisdiction that allow public authorities to access the transferred data (i.e for law enforcement, intelligence, administrative, and regulatory supervision purposes).                             "mandatory": false,

                            "description": "",
                            "additional_details": "As per the EDPB's latest guidance on international data transfers, the EDPB has suggested that contractual measures should be put in place to supplement the technical measures and legally obligate the data importer to take steps to protect the data.                             "number": 18,
                            "description": "",
                            "additional_details": "As per the EDPB's latest guidance on international data transfers, organizational measures which can be applied by the data exporters and imposed on data importers contribute to ensuring consistency in the protection of personal data during the full cycle of the processing, while improving risk awareness and the capacity to react to surveillance requests by public authorities.
